title: The Ultimate Test of Leadership: Do You Create More Leaders?
author: Parker Houston
summary: Parker Houston argues that the best measure of leadership is whether you create more leaders, building on a John Maxwell passage in which Maxwell found his influence growing only where he had developed potential leaders. Houston admits that in a busy executive role the first thing he cut was one-on-one time with his team, and that the work got less effective, not more. He says leaders who extend their influence through others multiply their impact, while those who do not risk believing no one else can do their job. He recommends developing a strong second-in-command and notes the joy of seeing mentees mentor others. He cites Google's Project Oxygen, where the best managers were emotionally stable, made time for one-on-ones, asked good questions and took an interest in people's lives, and Laszlo Bock's remark that technical expertise matters far less than accessibility. He ends with three actions: make the time, take a personal interest, and get a mentor yourself.
points: Developing leaders is a growth strategy for the leader: Maxwell found influence and productivity rose only where he invested in potential leaders.
Cutting one-on-one time under pressure is a mistake, because less time with the team makes a leader less effective.
A strong second-in-command lets a leader delegate with trust and gives others room to grow, at the cost of more time up front.
Google's Project Oxygen found that connection and accessibility beat deep technical expertise as marks of the best managers.
Taking personal interest in people and having a mentor yourself keeps ego in check and models how to spend time with your own team.
quotes: Good leaders create loyal followers. Great leaders create other leaders who surpass, and outlast them.
The irony is that the less time you spend with your team members, the less effective you are. You trade frenzied activity for real impact.

When you extend your influence through others, your impact is exponential. When you fail to tap into the power of your team, you also run the risk of starting to believe the lie that you are more important than you really are—that no one else can do what you do.
In my experience, there is always someone else who can do your job. You just can’t see them when you are eclipsing the spotlight.

The most effective leaders often develop a great second-in-command. Sometimes two or three of them. That way, when they start to become overwhelmed, they have other growing leaders who they can quickly delegate projects to.

They identified eight vital behaviors, but by far the most effective managers were emotionally stable people who made one-on-one time for their team members, asked good questions, and were interested in their lives.
It turns out that’s absolutely the least important thing. It’s important, but pales in comparison to just making a connection and being accessible.
Third, we often dramatically underestimate the need that others have to pass along their wisdom.
